idiom_name: `try { ... } finally { action() }` with an explicit commit flag (plus `using` where the runtime ships it)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no destructors, so the scope guard is written as try/finally - the finally block runs on normal exit, on `return` and on throw - with the release action moved into it and commit expressed by a flag or by a helper object that returns a dismiss closure. Where the Explicit Resource Management proposal is available (using / await using declarations, Symbol.dispose / Symbol.asyncDispose, DisposableStack, SuppressedError; shipped in Chromium 134 / V8 13.8 and Firefox 134, not in Safari and not in Node.js at the time of writing) the declarative form replaces the manual one: `using res = { [Symbol.dispose]() { ... } }` disposes in reverse order at scope exit. The classic guard class is worth writing only in a single fixed runtime where the same action is reused many times; otherwise `using` when available and try/finally everywhere are the honest realizations.
pitfalls: Errors raised inside the finally block replace the original error and a `return` inside it discards the pending result - exit actions must be non-throwing, and the same holds for JS's aggregated SuppressedError when disposers fail.

There is no compile-time or runtime check that a guard was written: a missing finally is a silent leak, and the guard only covers code inside the block, so resources acquired earlier are not protected.
A guard captured by a long-lived closure (listener, cache entry, promise callback) outlives its scope, so the exit action must be idempotent or the guard dismissed before the scope is left.

variants.name: `using` / `await using` declarations (Explicit Resource Management)
variants.implementation_notes: Declare the resource with `using r = ...` (or `await using` for objects providing [Symbol.asyncDispose]()) and the runtime calls the disposer when the enclosing block, function or module scope exits, in reverse order of declaration, regardless of the kind of exit; dynamically registered resources go through DisposableStack (use/adopt/defer/move/dispose), and disposal errors are aggregated into SuppressedError. Choose this variant where the engine ships the proposal - Chromium 134+ / V8 13.8 and Firefox 134 per the V8 feature page - and the resource is tied to one lexical scope; MDN still records the feature as limited availability, so libraries need a fallback or a build guard.
pitfalls: `using` may not appear at the top level of a script or of a `switch` (only blocks, functions and modules), and a closure that captures the binding observes it already disposed when it later runs - MDN documents this explicitly.
Support is uneven: Safari and Node.js had no support on the V8 feature page, so a library that requires `using` needs a documented runtime requirement or a try/finally fallback.

Disposal failures are not thrown one by one: every error is folded into a single SuppressedError whose error/suppressed fields must be inspected, otherwise the real failure looks like a cleanup failure.
